title: Wrathful Red Dragon + Blasphemous Act: does the sweeper become a table-kill?

stack.note: cast from hand for {R} (nine creatures on the battlefield reduce the {8} to nothing); about to resolve

extras.context: VERIFIED PRE-SWAP (Wrathful has since been promoted to the 99 — see HISTORY.md 2026-07-28); Blasphemous Act is maindeck. The sideboard analysis parked Wrathful behind exactly this question. Wrathful Red Dragon (5/5, Flying): 'Whenever a Dragon you control is dealt damage, it deals that much damage to any target that isn't a Dragon.' Blasphemous Act: 'Blasphemous Act deals 13 damage to each creature.' Your three Dragons are 5/5 (Wrathful), 4/4 (Ventmaw) and 7/7 (Gnawbone) — all three will be dealt lethal damage by the Act.

scenario.question: Resolve Blasphemous Act. The 13 damage is dealt to every creature simultaneously — including your three Dragons, all of which will die. How many of Wrathful Red Dragon's triggered abilities trigger, given the damaged Dragons (and Wrathful itself) are dealt lethal damage in the same event? Do Dragons that die to the 13 still produce redirect triggers, and what does 'it deals that much damage' mean for a source that is no longer on the battlefield? Can each redirect target a player, and may all of them target the same player? Walk the state-based actions and the trigger resolutions to the final life totals.

steps.action: Blasphemous Act resolves. Its oracle text reads 'Blasphemous Act deals 13 damage to each creature.' The 13 damage is dealt to all nine creatures on the battlefield — your Wrathful Red Dragon (5/5), Savage Ventmaw (4/4), and Old Gnawbone (7/7), Opponent A's five 1/1 Goblin tokens, and Opponent B's 3/3 — as a single simultaneous action.
steps.effect: 13 damage is marked on each of the nine creatures at the same time, in one event.

citations.quote: The controller of the spell or ability follows its instructions in the order written.
Some spells and abilities include actions taken on multiple players and/or objects. In most cases, each such action is processed simultaneously.

steps.action: Wrathful Red Dragon's ability ('Whenever a Dragon you control is dealt damage, it deals that much damage to any target that isn't a Dragon') checks the damage event. Wrathful is still on the battlefield at the moment the event occurs, and the one simultaneous event contains three occurrences of 'a Dragon you control is dealt damage': Wrathful itself, Savage Ventmaw, and Old Gnawbone. The opponents' creatures are not Dragons you control, so they produce no triggers.
steps.effect: The ability triggers three times — once for each of your three Dragons, including Wrathful being dealt damage itself. The triggers do nothing yet; they wait to be put on the stack.

citations.quote: Whenever a game event or game state matches a triggered ability’s trigger event, that ability automatically triggers. The ability doesn’t do anything at this point.
An ability triggers only once each time its trigger event occurs. However, it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences.

steps.action: State-based actions are checked before any player would receive priority — and therefore before the three triggers are put on the stack. Every creature on the battlefield has 13 damage marked, which meets or exceeds each one's toughness.
steps.effect: All nine creatures — Wrathful Red Dragon, Savage Ventmaw, Old Gnawbone, the five 1/1 Goblin tokens, and the 3/3 — are destroyed simultaneously as a single event. The battlefield is now empty of creatures.

citations.quote: If a creature has toughness greater than 0, it has damage marked on it, and the total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed.
the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event

steps.action: The three Wrathful Red Dragon triggers are put on the stack even though Wrathful (their source) and all three damaged Dragons are now in the graveyard. Triggered abilities that have already triggered exist independently of their source; you (their controller) put them on the stack in any order you choose after the state-based actions finish.
steps.effect: Three instances of 'it deals that much damage to any target that isn't a Dragon' go on the stack, in an order of your choice.

citations.quote: Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source. Destruction or removal of the source after that time won’t affect the ability.

Each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event (see rule 704, “State-Based Actions”), then repeats this process until no state-based actions are performed. Then triggered abilities are put on the stack
each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isn’t another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose.

steps.action: Targets are chosen as each trigger is put on the stack, following the same process as casting a spell. 'Any target' means a creature, player, planeswalker, or battle — but because the state-based actions in step 3 already destroyed every creature, no creatures remain to target. Each opponent (and you) is a legal non-Dragon target. Each of the three triggers is a separate ability choosing its own target, so all three may legally choose the same player.
steps.effect: You choose targets: all three triggers target Opponent A (32 life). (The alternative — all three at Opponent B — is analyzed in the answer.) Legal targets exist, so no trigger is removed from the stack.

citations.quote: The remainder of the process for putting a triggered ability on the stack is identical to the process for casting a spell listed in rules 601.2c–d. If a choice is required when the triggered ability goes on the stack but no legal choices can be made for it, or if a rule or a continuous effect otherwise makes the ability illegal, the ability is simply removed from the stack.
These targets may be creatures, players, planeswalkers, or battles.
The player announces their choice of an appropriate object or player for each target the spell requires.

steps.action: The triggers resolve one at a time (top-down). Each says the damaged Dragon — not the ability — deals 13 damage to the target. Those Dragons are no longer on the battlefield, so the game uses their last known information; a source that has left the battlefield can still perform the action. 'That much damage' is 13 in each case, the amount dealt to that Dragon.
steps.effect: Each resolving trigger has a dead Dragon (via last known information) deal 13 damage to Opponent A, causing 13 life loss per trigger: 32 → 19 → 6 → −7.

citations.quote: if the source is no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in at that time, its last known information is used. The source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists.
Damage dealt to a player normally causes that player to lose that much life.

steps.action: State-based actions are checked again after the triggers resolve (in a multiplayer game, as soon as Opponent A's life total is 0 or less at an SBA check, they lose — in practice after the trigger that takes them below 0 resolves).
steps.effect: Opponent A, at −7 life, loses the game. Opponent B is untouched at 40 life with an empty board.

citations.quote: If a player has 0 or less life, that player loses the game.

final_state.summary: Blasphemous Act destroys all nine creatures (including all three of your Dragons) in one SBA event; Wrathful Red Dragon still yields exactly three redirect triggers, each dealing 13 via last known information. 39 total redirect damage kills the 32-life opponent but cannot also kill the 40-life opponent.

opponents.status: loses the game (all three triggers targeted at them)
alive; board empty (3/3 destroyed); would be at 1 life in the alternative line where all three triggers target them instead

resolution.answer: Not a table-kill, but a one-player kill plus a full sweep. Exactly THREE triggers occur — one per Dragon you control dealt damage, including Wrathful itself (603.2c: one event, three occurrences), and they trigger even though every Dragon dies to the same event, because the triggers exist independently of their sources once the event has occurred (113.7a). 'It deals that much damage' means the dead Dragon itself deals 13, using last known information — a source can still deal damage after it no longer exists (113.7a). All creatures die to the lethal-damage SBA (704.5g) BEFORE targets are chosen, so the only legal non-Dragon targets are players; each trigger targets independently and all three may target the same player. That yields 3 × 13 = 39 redirect damage: enough to kill the 32-life opponent exactly (needs all three; two triggers = 26 falls short), or to drop the 40-life opponent to 1 — but never both. Wrathful Red Dragon turns Blasphemous Act into 'destroy everything, one opponent of your choice at ≤39 life dies' — excellent, but with only three Dragons in play it is not a table-kill against these life totals.

findings.note: Resolution follows instructions in order written; verbatim quote.
Damage to all nine creatures processed simultaneously as one action; full rule confirms.
Ability triggers automatically on the damage event and does nothing yet.
One event, three occurrences of 'a Dragon you control is dealt damage' (incl. Wrathful itself) = three triggers; rule's mass-destruction example is directly analogous.
13 >= toughness of every creature (max 7); all nine destroyed by lethal-damage SBA.
SBAs performed simultaneously as a single event before triggers are put on the stack; ordering claim matches full rule.
Triggered abilities exist independently of their destroyed source.
SBA loop completes, then triggered abilities go on the stack.
Controller places their triggers in any order they choose (APNAP two-part process; single controller here).
Targeting follows 601.2c-d when the trigger is put on the stack; removal-if-no-legal-targets caveat correctly not triggered since players are legal.
'Any target' = creatures, players, planeswalkers, battles; with all creatures dead and no PWs/battles, only players remain, and no player is a Dragon.
Each trigger is a separate instance of 'target'; three separate abilities may all choose the same player.
LKI: the dead Dragon (source) can still perform the action; 'that much damage' = 13 per Dragon. 32->19->6->-7 arithmetic correct.
Damage to a player causes that much life loss.
Player at 0 or less life loses; SBA check after the trigger that takes A below 0. -7 correct.

checker.summary: ITERATION 2: pass. Both iteration-1 card-fact defects are fixed and consistent everywhere: 'nine creatures' now appears in step 1, step 3, and the final summary (3 Dragons + 5 Goblin tokens + one 3/3 = 9), and the scenario stack note now reads cast for {R} with nine creatures reducing the {8} to nothing, matching Blasphemous Act's oracle text in cards.json ({8}{R}, {1} less per creature). Mechanical gate passes. All 14 citations re-verified from scratch against full rule text: supported. Card facts verified: Wrathful Red Dragon 5/5 Flying sideboard card with exact quoted ability; Savage Ventmaw 4/4 Dragon; Old Gnawbone 7/7 Dragon; Blasphemous Act maindeck sorcery. Missing-step audit clean: SBA destruction correctly ordered before trigger placement (704.3/117.5), LKI handled for dead damage sources (113.7a), target legality holds at each resolution (A at 19 then 6 when later triggers resolve), no other triggered abilities implicated (Ventmaw/Gnawbone triggers are attack/combat-damage only), and both arithmetic chains (32->19->6->-7; 40-39=1; 2 triggers = 26 < 32) check out. The headline conclusion — three triggers, 39 redirect damage, one-player kill plus full sweep, not a table-kill — is rules-correct.

presentable_note: Held back on the v1.0.0 baseline: the rules finding stands and the checker's verdict is unchanged, but this board names Savage Ventmaw, Blasphemous Act — no longer in the 99, so the deck can no longer make it. Not withdrawn: a passing stack is a fact about how a board resolves, and that does not expire when a card leaves.
